scenes.narration: Say you keep ten million phone numbers, and you need to find one of them, again and again, thousands of times a second.

steps.say: In a list with no order, you may have to check every one of the ten million.
Sort the list and you can halve it on each check, so twenty four checks are enough.
That is fast. But when a busy system does this thousands of times a second, even twenty four checks add up.
What we want is one jump, straight to the spot where the number lives.
No scanning, no halving. That is what a hash table gives you.

scenes.title: Working out where "cat" goes
scenes.narration: The trick is to work out the spot from the key itself. The rule that does this is called a hash function.

steps.say: Our key is the word cat.
Every letter is stored as a number. C is 99, a is 97, and t is 116.
Add them up, and you get 312.
The table has only eight slots, so we keep the remainder after dividing by eight. 312 divided by eight leaves 0.
So cat goes in slot zero.
To find cat later, we do not search. We do the same sum, get zero again, and read slot zero.

scenes.title: "act" lands on the same slot
scenes.narration: Now add a second word, act.

steps.say: It has the same letters as the first word, in a different order, so its sum is also 312.
And the remainder is zero again, so act points at slot zero.
But cat is already there. Two different keys want the same slot. This is called a collision.
You cannot avoid it. There are endless possible words, and only eight slots.
Put ten pigeons in nine holes, and some hole gets two.

scenes.title: Each slot holds a short list
scenes.narration: The first fix is called chaining.

steps.say: Each slot holds the start of a small linked list instead of one key. Slot zero points at a node holding cat.
When act collides with it, act just joins the end of that list.
To find act, jump to slot zero, then walk the list until you meet act. Here that is two checks.

scenes.title: Take the next free slot
scenes.narration: The second fix is called open addressing. Every key lives in the table itself.

steps.say: Act starts at slot zero, its hash.
Slot zero is taken by cat.
So it steps to the next slot, slot one, which is free, and act goes there.
To find act later, start at slot zero, see cat, and step along until you meet act or an empty slot.

labels.old: seven keys sit in eight slots

scenes.narration: With chaining, the danger is a crowded table. Here seven keys sit in eight slots, and each list hangs below its slot.

steps.say: The load factor is the number of keys divided by the number of slots. Seven over eight is zero point eight seven five.
The keys do not spread out evenly, so the lists grow. Slot zero holds 3 keys.
Finding pig means walking past the two keys in front of it.
So the table grows. We make a new one with twice the slots, sixteen.
Then every key is hashed again, with the remainder after dividing by sixteen, and moves to its new slot.
Most lists shrink to one key. But cat and act still share slot eight, because their sums are equal whatever the size.
Real hash functions mix in the order of the letters, so this happens far less.

scenes.narration: Many tables grow once the load factor passes about two thirds to three quarters.

steps.say: Then the lists stay short, and every operation is one jump plus a check or two.
On average, looking up, adding and removing all take the same short time, however big the table gets.
The worst case is every key in one slot, which a good hash function makes very unlikely.
Growing the table is slow when it happens, but it happens so rarely that it adds only a little to each insert on average.

draw.write: growing: rare, so cheap on average

steps.say: That is how dictionaries, database indexes and caches answer in an instant.
